title: Everyone has an hour (Avot 4:3)
hookLine: despise no one and dismiss nothing; every person has their hour and every thing its place
tomorrow: why does one rabbi say 'very' twice?

cards: Every group chat has someone who barely posts, and every team has someone who stays on the bench. Ben Azzai has a word for them, and for us. Do not despise any person, he says, and do not dismiss any thing.
For there is no person who doesn't have their hour, and no thing that doesn't have its place.

teach.b: Readers have heard this two ways, and both live inside the tradition.
The first reading is respect. Every person matters now, whatever their hour; the hour is only when the rest of us finally notice.
The Mishnah backs it elsewhere, in Sanhedrin: humanity began with a single person, it says, so that no one could ever tell another, my father is greater than yours.
At its best: if everyone comes from one ancestor, there's no one left to look down on. The second reading is caution.

Don't despise anyone, because their hour will come, and you may need them, or answer to them, when it does. At its best: it's honest about people, and humility about the future can still produce real respect.
Ben Azzai's words hold both. Everyone has an hour can be a promise to the overlooked, or a warning to the proud.
And the second half matters too: no thing without its place.
Nothing in the world is junk, either.

how: Avot 4:3 is learned with Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, which says humanity began with one person so no one could claim a greater ancestor.

games.q: what does “everyone has an hour” mean?
o: each person has their own time to matter
a set hour each day for prayer and study
the time limit on a turn to speak

games.q: Ben Azzai's two halves — tap the pairs.

s: Ben Azzai says some people just aren't worth noticing
there is no person who doesn't have their hour.
the Mishnah says humanity began with one person so no one could say 'my father is greater'
the saying is about people only, not things
no thing without its place, too.

games.q: a friend says 'everyone has an hour' is just strategy: be nice to people because they might be useful. what's the best case for her reading?
o: it's honest: humility about who'll matter later can still grow real respect.
it proves kindness is fake, so there's no real point to being kind.
it means only people who become important deserve any respect.
games.why: the caution reading is inside the tradition too. the respect reading leans on Sanhedrin: one ancestor for all, so no one is greater by birth.

practice: Look at one ordinary object near you: a chair, a cup, a light switch. Somebody you'll never meet designed it, made it, carried it, put it there. Let the sit be a quiet thank-you to the hands nobody saw.

wordCard.voice: Everyone has an hour. Ben Azzai's sha'ah: no person without their time, no thing without its place.

orig.note: Hebrew: an hour, a moment; Ben Azzai's word for each person's time.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone has an hour. No person despised, and nothing dismissed. See you soon.

sources.ref: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (one first person, so no one says 'my father is greater')
